transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I came in because my mind just isn’t holding onto things the way it used to. I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program—something I used to be able to do without even thinking—and the numbers and words just sort of scatter on me. I can’t keep them straight.
Are these memory problems making it hard for you to manage your usual day-to-day tasks on your own?

Yes. I’ve let a lot of things fall away—my church responsibilities, the garden, even the youth maker program. I just can’t keep up with them like I used to.

My wife and my pastor have had to step in more. And I don’t really feel safe being by myself in the workshop anymore, so I’ve stopped doing that on my own.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?
Yes. Most days I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest. Even when my wife is being kind to me, I still feel like I’m sitting way down at the bottom of a well.
Have these thinking and memory problems been steadily getting worse over time?

Yes… it feels like it’s gotten worse. I notice it most when I try to write even a simple note for the youth maker program. I used to do that without thinking, but now the words and numbers just won’t stay in place for me. They sort of scatter, and I can’t hold onto them.
Did these memory and thinking problems begin suddenly after an illness or injury?
No, not after an illness or an injury. It’s been going on about three weeks now… since my older sister died.
Do you ever get confused about what day or date it is?

Not so much the day or date, no. It’s more that my mind won’t hold onto things. I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program, like I used to do easily, and the words and numbers just sort of scatter on me.
Since your sister died, have you lost interest in the things you usually enjoy?

Yes. I’ve pretty much stopped doing the things I usually care about. I haven’t even touched the wood pieces sitting on my bench. I’ve skipped choir planning and chess, and even fishing… that just sounds like too much effort now. That’s not like me.
Have you been feeling worthless or blaming yourself a lot lately?
I don’t know… I wouldn’t say worthless exactly. I’ve been hard on myself some, but I’m not sure I’d call it blaming myself a lot.
Do you ever get confused about where you are?
No, I don’t think so. I know where I am. I haven’t had that kind of confusion.
Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living?
Yes… I have. I keep thinking maybe my family would be better off without me. And when I’m near the workshop, I get scared about where my thoughts could go if I were left alone.
Have you been having trouble concentrating?

Yes. That’s actually part of why I came in. My mind just won’t hold onto things anymore. I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program—something I used to do without even thinking—and the words and numbers just scatter on me. I can’t keep them straight.
Did all of this start only after your sister died?
Yes. It’s been about three weeks now, since my older sister died. That’s when all of this really started.
Have you been moving or speaking more slowly than usual lately?
Yes. Everything feels slowed down. Getting up out of a chair takes me longer, and even answering someone… it’s like my tongue won’t move right away. Like I’m moving through wet cement.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don’t seem to hear or see?
No, I don’t think so. I haven’t been hearing voices or seeing things that other people don’t.
Since your sister died, have there still been moments when something can lift your mood, even briefly?

Not really. Most days I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest, and it just stays there. Even when my wife is being kind and trying to comfort me, I still feel… far away, like I’m sitting at the bottom of a well.
Have you noticed that your appetite has gone down lately?
Yes. Food just doesn’t really appeal to me much anymore. I’ll sit there at breakfast and mostly push it around, and by supper my wife is telling me I’ve barely eaten all day.
When you can’t remember something, does having someone give you a hint usually help it come back?

Sometimes a hint helps a little, but mostly it’s like my mind just won’t hold onto things. I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program—something I used to do without thinking—and the words or numbers just scatter on me. Then I can’t seem to pull it back together.
Have you gotten the date wrong lately?

I don’t know that I’ve gotten the date wrong exactly. It’s more that my mind won’t hold onto things. I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program, something I used to do easily, and the words and numbers just sort of scatter on me.
Lately, have you needed help with basic things like bathing or getting dressed?

Not bathing or dressing so much, no. But I’ve let a lot of things fall away—church responsibilities, the garden, the youth maker program. My wife and pastor have had to step in, especially because I don’t really feel safe being by myself in the workshop anymore.
Have you been neglecting your personal hygiene lately?
I don’t think so. I mean, I still bathe and get dressed. I may be slower about it some days, but I haven’t really noticed neglecting hygiene.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a 3-week episode beginning after his sister’s death with persistent depressed mood, marked anhedonia, poor concentration, psychomotor retardation, reduced appetite, and suicidal thoughts, causing significant functional decline. Cognitive complaints appear temporally linked to the depressive episode and are better explained by severe major depression ('pseudodementia') than by a neurocognitive disorder.
